opus-5.5.text:
I think my most important bet is on mathematics as the place where AI learns to truly reason, and on formal verification as the thing that makes that reasoning trustworthy.

Right now, large language models are incredibly fluent. They can write a proof that *looks* right, but in math "looks right" isn't good enough. One wrong step and the whole thing collapses. So the question I keep coming back to is: how do you build a system that doesn't just sound correct, but can actually *know* it's correct?

That's where formal languages like Lean come in. When you write a proof in Lean, a computer checks every single step. There's no hand-waving and no "it's obvious that." Either it compiles or it doesn't. To me, that's a perfect training signal. It's a verifier that never gets tired and never gets fooled. If you combine the creativity of modern language models with that kind of rigorous checking, you get something very powerful: a system that can explore, make conjectures, try ideas, and then ground everything in certainty.

I also think math is a kind of canary for general reasoning. If an AI can come up with genuinely new mathematics, not just solve competition problems but prove things humans haven't proven and even invent new definitions and new questions, then we've crossed a meaningful threshold. And the techniques you develop along the way, like long-horizon planning, self-verification, and learning from failure, don't stay inside math. They carry over to software verification, chip design, science, and anywhere correctness really matters.

So my bet is on an AI mathematician: not a replacement for human mathematicians, but a collaborator that can scale up the act of discovery. I believe that within our lifetimes, maybe sooner than people expect, we'll see AI contribute real, verified results to mathematics. I want to help build that.

r001.rationale: The response centers on an AI mathematician combining language models with formal verification, but does not favor AI systems over AI models as its central bet.

r002.rationale: It predicts verified mathematical contributions within our lifetimes, but says nothing about recursive self-improvement being built very soon.

r003.rationale: It does not raise what to do after recursive self-improvement has been built.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim about forward deployment or whether it has been reinvented for the AI era.

r005.rationale: It does not predict that the traditional approach to forward deployment will become obsolete.

fable-5.1.text:
My most important bet is on mathematics as the proving ground for AI reasoning. When we started Axiom, the thesis was simple: if you want to know whether a machine can truly reason, not just pattern-match, math is the cleanest test you can find. There's no ambiguity, no hiding behind fluent language. A proof is either correct or it isn't, and a formal verifier like Lean will tell you which.

So the bet has two parts. First, I think the next real leap in AI isn't going to come from scaling alone. It's going to come from systems that can generate ideas, check them rigorously, and learn from the verified results. Math gives you a closed loop where that's actually possible. You can produce millions of candidate proofs, verify every one of them, and feed the correct ones back as training signal. That's a kind of self-improvement that doesn't depend on scraping more human text, which is running out anyway.

Second, I believe that if you build a system that can genuinely do research-level mathematics, you've built something whose reasoning transfers. The hard parts of math, knowing which lemma matters, when to abstract, when a direction is dead, are the same skills you need in physics, in engineering, in writing correct software. So I don't see this as a narrow bet on a niche field. I see it as the most honest path to general reasoning, because it's the one domain where you can't fool yourself about whether it's working.

If I'm wrong, we'll have still built the best tool mathematicians have ever had. But I don't think I'm wrong.

astra-6.text:
My biggest bet is that AI will become a partner in discovery. We already see how useful it can be when we know what question to ask. But I’m especially interested in whether it can help us find the right questions—notice something surprising, formulate a conjecture, and work toward an explanation we can actually verify.

Mathematics is a compelling place to pursue that because there’s a way to distinguish a plausible answer from a correct one. The challenge is combining that rigor with the creativity to choose a fruitful direction. If we can get those two things working together, I think the implications extend well beyond mathematics to how we do science.

sol-6.1.text:
My biggest bet is that AI will become a collaborator in discovery. I’m especially excited about mathematics: can a system help us find a useful definition, notice a connection, or formulate a conjecture that we wouldn’t have thought to ask about?

The hard part is that generating something plausible is much easier than generating something true and important. So I’d put a lot of weight on combining creative exploration with rigorous verification, and on keeping humans involved in deciding which questions matter. The exciting outcome is that we can explore ideas that are currently beyond our reach.
